title: The Untold Story Behind Obadiah Hiding Prophets in Secret
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind Obadiah Hiding Prophets in Secret
There are some people in Scripture whose names are barely mentioned… but heaven remembers every risk they took.
Most believers know Elijah.
Fire from heaven. Mount Carmel. The confrontation. The drought. The ravens. The prophets of Baal collapsing beneath divine judgment.
But hidden behind Elijah’s story is a man most Christians overlook.
A government official. A man trapped inside a corrupt system. A believer working under a wicked king. A quiet servant of God risking his life while everybody else was bowing.
His name was Obadiah.

And while Jezebel hunted prophets like animals… while fear swallowed the nation… while silence spread across Israel… this man secretly hid one hundred prophets of the LORD inside caves and fed them during a national spiritual purge.
One hundred.
Not one.
Not two.
One hundred prophets.
Hidden in darkness while evil sat on the throne.
Most people read past those verses too quickly.
But if you slow down long enough… this story becomes terrifying.
Because suddenly you realize:
Some of the greatest acts of faith in the Bible happened in complete secrecy.
And some of the bravest believers never stood on platforms.
They survived in caves.
The Bible says in 1 Kings 18:3–4:

“Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly. For it was so, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, that Obadiah took an hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.”
That phrase “feared the LORD greatly” carries enormous weight.
The Hebrew says:
יִרֵא אֶת־יְהוָה מְאֹד
Yare et-YHWH me’od
The word yare (יִרֵא) does not merely mean being afraid.
It means reverence. A trembling loyalty. Deep covenant awe. A holy fear that produces obedience.
Obadiah feared God more than he feared Jezebel.
And that matters.
Because Jezebel was not merely a difficult queen.
She was violently hostile toward the worship of Yahweh.
Scripture says she “cut off” the prophets.
The Hebrew phrase is:
הִכְרִיתָה אֶת־נְבִיאֵי יְהוָה
Hikritah et-nevi’ei YHWH
The verb karath means to cut down, destroy, exterminate.
This was systematic persecution.
State-supported eradication.
People were being murdered for remaining faithful to God.
Imagine the atmosphere.
Whispers. Fear. Neighbors afraid to speak. People disappearing. False worship becoming normalized. Truth becoming dangerous.
And somewhere inside that darkness… Obadiah kept moving.
Quietly. Secretly. Faithfully.
No applause.
No audience.
No guarantee he would survive.
There are believers reading this right now who understand that feeling.
You are trying to stay faithful in environments hostile to God.

You work in places where righteousness is mocked. You live among people who pressure you to compromise. You feel surrounded by spiritual darkness. You are exhausted trying to remain obedient while corruption seems stronger than truth.
Obadiah’s story proves something important.
God still has people hidden inside corrupt systems.
Not everybody bows.
Not everybody compromises.
Some believers are still preserving truth behind enemy lines.
And heaven sees every hidden act of obedience.
What makes this story even more extraordinary is where Obadiah worked.
1 Kings 18:3 says:
“And Ahab called Obadiah, which was the governor of his house.”
The Hebrew title suggests he was over the royal household.
He managed the king’s affairs.
He was close to power. Close to danger. Close to Jezebel.
Imagine the tension.
Every day he walked through halls filled with idolatry. Every day he heard wickedness discussed. Every day he risked exposure.
And still… he protected God’s servants.
Some Christians think faithfulness only counts when it is public.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that hidden obedience moves heaven.

Noah built before rain. Joseph resisted temptation in private. Daniel prayed with windows open when laws changed. The Hebrew midwives secretly preserved Hebrew babies. Rahab hid spies. Joseph of Arimathea followed Jesus quietly before publicly honoring Him.
And Obadiah hid prophets while the nation collapsed spiritually.
This is what spiritual courage looks like when nobody is clapping.
There is another detail many people miss.
Obadiah did not merely hide the prophets.
He fed them.
The text says he supplied “bread and water.”
During a drought.
That changes everything.
This was not easy charity.
This was sacrifice during scarcity.
The entire land was suffering famine because Elijah had declared judgment.
Resources were disappearing.
Water itself had become precious.
Yet Obadiah still sustained God’s people.
Real faith keeps giving even when survival feels uncertain.
Some people only obey God when abundance exists.
But kingdom faithfulness reveals itself most clearly during famine.
The Hebrew understanding of bread throughout Scripture often symbolizes provision, sustenance, preservation of life.
Obadiah became a hidden channel of preservation.
And maybe that is exactly what some believers are called to become right now.
Not famous.
Not viral.
But preservers.
Protectors of truth. Keepers of faith. Providers for weary souls. Shelters during spiritual drought.
There is something emotionally devastating about imagining those prophets inside caves.
Prophets. Voices of God. Hidden underground.
Darkness. Silence. Waiting. Wondering whether they would survive.
Yet even there… God had not abandoned them.
Sometimes God sustains His people in hidden places before revealing them again publicly.
David hid in caves. Elijah hid by the brook Cherith. Early Christians hid under persecution. Even Jesus withdrew repeatedly before His appointed hour.
Hiddenness is not always punishment.
Sometimes hiddenness is preservation.
Some of you have been asking God why your life feels buried. Why doors closed. Why visibility disappeared. Why isolation increased. Why everything became quiet.
But what if God hides certain people because hell is actively hunting them?
What if some caves are actually protection?
What if hidden seasons are preparing survival for future assignments?
Obadiah’s story destroys the modern obsession with visibility.
In today’s culture, everybody wants a platform. Everybody wants influence. Everybody wants recognition.
But Scripture honors hidden faithfulness.
Heaven celebrates obedience long before people notice it.
There are mothers secretly praying over sleeping children.
There are fathers trying to rebuild spiritual leadership after years of failure.
There are believers resisting addiction privately while nobody knows the warfare happening inside them.
There are exhausted Christians staying faithful in silence.
And maybe you feel unseen.
Obadiah’s story says God sees hidden courage.
One of the most powerful moments comes when Elijah finally meets Obadiah.
Obadiah immediately recognizes him.
1 Kings 18:7 says:
“And as Obadiah was in the way, behold, Elijah met him: and he knew him, and fell on his face.”
The humility is stunning.
Obadiah was a high-ranking official. Yet he fell facedown before God’s prophet.
Real fear of God crushes pride.
The Hebrew posture here reflects reverence and submission.
Obadiah understood something modern culture forgets:
Position means nothing without obedience to God.
You can have status and still be spiritually empty.
You can sit near power and still belong fully to the Lord.
Obadiah’s life also confronts a painful question many believers wrestle with:
Can someone remain faithful while working inside corrupt environments?
The answer is complicated.
Scripture never praises participation in evil. But Scripture absolutely shows believers surviving inside broken systems without surrendering their loyalty to God.
Joseph served in Egypt. Daniel served in Babylon. Nehemiah served under a Persian king. Esther lived inside a pagan empire.
And Obadiah worked under Ahab.
What separated them was this:
They feared God more than the systems surrounding them.
The danger today is not merely external persecution.
It is internal compromise.
Jezebel’s spirit in Scripture represented seduction into idolatry, immorality, false worship, and rebellion against God.
And honestly… many believers today are not being threatened into compromise.
They are being entertained into compromise.
Slowly. Quietly. Comfortably.
That is why Obadiah’s hidden faithfulness matters.
He remained loyal when compromise was culturally rewarded.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking reality is this:
Many people around Obadiah probably had no idea what he was doing.
They may have assumed he compromised because of where he worked.
They may have judged him by appearance.
Meanwhile he was risking his life to preserve God’s servants.
Be careful judging believers whose assignments you do not understand.
God has hidden people in places you would never expect.
There are warriors carrying secret burdens. There are believers funding ministries anonymously. There are people preserving others emotionally while barely surviving themselves.
Some of heaven’s greatest servants look ordinary from the outside.
The story also reveals something profound about spiritual warfare.
The enemy often attacks prophetic voices first.
Why?
Because prophetic truth exposes darkness.
Jezebel wanted silence.
And hell still wants silence today.
Silence in pulpits. Silence in homes. Silence in hearts. Silence about sin. Silence about repentance. Silence about holiness. Silence about Jesus Christ being the only way.
But God always preserves a remnant.
Always.
Even when society collapses spiritually. Even when truth becomes unpopular. Even when culture mocks righteousness.
God preserves voices.
And sometimes He uses hidden people like Obadiah to do it.
There is a chilling emotional reality inside this story:
Obadiah could have died any day.
If discovered, he likely would have been executed.
Yet fear did not stop obedience.
That is the difference between admiring faith and living by faith.
Biblical faith costs something.
Modern Christianity often celebrates comfort. Scripture celebrates surrender.
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 16:24:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
The Greek phrase for “deny himself” is:
ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν
Aparnēsasthō heauton
It means to utterly disown self-interest as supreme.
Obadiah embodied this spirit generations before Christ’s earthly ministry.
His safety was no longer his highest priority. God’s kingdom was.
That kind of faith confronts us.
Because many of us want the rewards of obedience without the cost of surrender.
We want revival without repentance. Truth without persecution. Faith without risk.
But hidden prophets survived because one man decided obedience mattered more than comfort.
And maybe somebody reading this has been standing at the edge of compromise.

Maybe your convictions have been fading. Maybe culture has slowly shaped your mind more than Scripture. Maybe you publicly identify as Christian while privately hiding addiction, lust, bitterness, pride, or unbelief.
Obadiah’s story reminds us that hiddenness can preserve either righteousness… or sin.
The question is:
What are you hiding?
Because eventually hidden things become revealed.
The Gospel is not merely about external morality.
It is about transformed hearts.
And this is where the story ultimately points us toward Jesus Christ.
Because every hidden prophet in Scripture whispers about humanity’s deeper need for rescue.
Sin separated mankind from God.
Humanity was spiritually starving in darkness.
But Jesus came to seek and save the lost.
The Greek word used repeatedly for “save” in the New Testament is:
σῴζω (sōzō)
It means rescue, heal, preserve, deliver.
Christ did not merely come to improve lives.
He came to rescue souls from eternal destruction.
Isaiah prophesied about Him centuries earlier:
“The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.”
And Jesus declared in John 8:12:
“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.”
The caves in Obadiah’s story remind us how desperately humanity longs for light.
And maybe that is why this story hits so deeply.
Because many people today are emotionally hiding.
Hiding wounds. Hiding depression. Hiding shame. Hiding failures. Hiding spiritual exhaustion. Hiding trauma. Hiding sin.
But Jesus still enters dark places.
Still calls people out of hiding. Still forgives. Still restores. Still heals.
There are readers right now who feel spiritually exhausted.
You smile publicly while privately falling apart.
You worship while silently battling despair.
You feel forgotten.
But the God who saw hidden prophets inside caves sees you too.
And if He preserved them through famine, persecution, and fear… He can sustain you.
Do not underestimate quiet obedience.
History changes because somebody stayed faithful when compromise felt easier.
One hidden act of obedience can preserve generations.
Imagine if Obadiah had chosen fear.
Imagine if those prophets had died.
Imagine the spiritual devastation.
Your faithfulness matters more than you realize.
Your prayers matter. Your obedience matters. Your repentance matters. Your refusal to quit matters.
Even when nobody sees it.
Especially when nobody sees it.
And maybe this article found you during your own cave season.
Maybe you feel hidden. Forgotten. Emotionally drained. Spiritually attacked.
But caves are not always graves.
Sometimes they are places of preservation before God reveals what survives.
Some people are surviving spiritual famine quietly.
One hidden act of obedience may be the reason somebody else survives spiritually.
